title: Best Business Security Cameras for Small Shops and Offices
excerpt: Which cameras suit shop tills, sales floors, stockrooms and rear doors — plus recording storage, night views and staff notice explained for owners.
body:
When a customer insists they paid with a fifty rather than a twenty, or a box of stock vanishes from a shelf nobody admits to touching, that is the moment a small shop owner wishes a camera had been watching. The best business security cameras for small shops and offices are the ones positioned to settle exactly these everyday disputes: a clear view of the till, the entrance, and the stockroom, with footage you can pull up the next morning.

This guide is for corner shops, cafés, salons, and small offices — not warehouses or chains. The aim is cameras covering the spots where money and goods change hands, recording through a full trading week without demanding constant attention.

Start with the till, not the front door

Most first-time buyers point their best camera at the front door and aim a cheap leftover at the register. Flip that priority. Door footage tells you who walked in; till footage tells you what happened where cash, cards, refunds, and voids are handled. Mount a compact indoor camera above and slightly behind the till, angled down so it sees hands, the drawer, and the customer's side of the counter. For help matching camera types to each position, see our small-business camera guide.

Dome cameras for the sales floor, bullet cameras for the back alley

Camera shape is not cosmetic — it signals where each type works best. Domes suit indoor ceilings: their smoked housing hides where the lens points, and the low profile survives knocks from ladders and lifted stock boxes.

Where domes earn their place

Use domes over the sales floor, the till, and office corridors. One wide view covers a whole room from a corner mount, and the hidden lens direction creates uncertainty across a wide area — useful when you cannot afford a camera per aisle.

Where bullet cameras do better

Use bullets for the rear delivery door, the alley, and any outdoor approach. Their housing shades the lens from rain glare, and their visible, directional shape reads as a deliberate warning above a back door. Mount under eaves or a canopy to keep rain and spiders off the lens.

Why shops outgrow wireless cameras fast

A single battery camera over a stockroom door is a fine stopgap, but shops scale past wireless quickly: four or five Wi-Fi cameras uploading clips all day will stutter on a basic broadband router already serving a card machine and customer Wi-Fi. For a permanent setup, wired cameras that carry power and video over one cable to a central recorder are the workhorse choice — one recorder under the counter, and footage that keeps recording even when the broadband drops. If drilling is impossible in a leased unit, limit wireless to two or three cameras on a separate network name and test the live view from the farthest corner first.

How much recording time a shop actually needs

A home camera that keeps three days of clips is fine; a shop that discovers a stock discrepancy on Friday needs last Monday still on disk. Choose a recorder or base station whose storage can expand, and run continuous recording on the till and entrance cameras with motion-only recording elsewhere. After a week of normal trading, check the retention screen confirms a full trading week or more of history, and note the figure on a label stuck to the recorder. If storage fees concern you, our no-subscription camera guide explains local recording options that avoid monthly fees.

Telling staff about cameras without killing morale

Cameras in staff areas succeed or fail on trust. Tell employees plainly where cameras are and that footage exists to resolve disputes fairly — including disputes where the recording clears the employee. Cover tills, stockrooms, and entrances; never toilets, changing areas, or break rooms. Laws on workplace recording and audio capture vary by state and country, so check the rules for your own jurisdiction before enabling microphones.

A short shopping checklist before you buy

  • Coverage first: till, entrance, stockroom, rear door — in that order of priority.
  • Wired where possible: one cable per camera back to a single recorder.
  • Expandable storage: confirm a full trading week or more of retention after real use.
  • Night check: review faces at the entrance after dark before finalising positions.
  • Staff notice: written, specific about locations, with private areas excluded.
  • Remote access: confirm viewing works on mobile data, not just shop Wi-Fi.

Buy for the disputes you already have — till disagreements, missing stock, after-hours visitors — and point every camera at a lesson learned rather than a guess.
